question: us-policy-positions:housing-land-use.right-to-counsel-in-eviction
definition: yes (preempts false) = a statewide law in force on 1/1/2026 gives eligible tenants a right to a lawyer in eviction cases (reach noted); no (preempts false) = no statewide right, cities may create their own; no (preempts true) = state bars local rights (none found).
summarySource: NCCRC 'Enacted Eviction Right to Counsel and Eviction Defense Programs' matrix (last modified August/September 2026; lists 5 statewide RTC laws: WA, MD, CT, MN, NE, plus Delaware as an eviction defense program), with state code pages for WA, MD, MN, NE, DE fetched 9/28/2026.

US-CT.note: Income-eligible tenants (at or below 80% of state median income) get a lawyer in eviction (summary process) and subsidy-termination proceedings through a Judicial Branch program launched January 2022 and phased in by the administering entity; the state code site (cga.ct.gov) failed TLS verification, so the NCCRC matrix is the source.

US-DE.note: Tenants at or below 200% of the federal poverty level have a statutory right to legal representation, but a legal aid provider may decline a case it finds lacks merit, small pro se landlords are excluded, and § 5607 phases it in through June 30, 2028 subject to funding.

US-MD.note: Tenants with household income at or below 50% of state median income have access to a lawyer in eviction and subsidy-termination proceedings, run by the Maryland Legal Services Corporation and phased in subject to funding (enacted 2021).

US-MN.note: Narrow reach: only public housing tenants facing a breach-of-lease eviction who cannot afford counsel get a court-appointed lawyer (enacted 2023 c 52); other tenants have no statewide right.

US-NE.note: Very narrow reach: only public housing residents in a city of the metropolitan class (currently only Omaha) get a court-appointed lawyer, paid by the housing agency, in termination hearings and related evictions (Laws 2024, LB840); no right for other tenants.

conflicts.readings: Statute 25 Del. C. § 5602 grants eligible tenants a 'right to legal representation' (answered yes); the NCCRC matrix classifies Delaware as an 'eviction defense program' rather than a right to counsel because providers may decline cases on merits and funding limits apply (reading no).
